Furthermore, we discuss an important extension to a broader class of spaces known as Gelfand triples, where we also establish the codiskyclicity of operators on these spaces. Moreover, we investigate the relationship between codiskyclicity and approximate codiskyclicity, demonstrating that they are equivalent properties. Finally, we examine the connection between codiskyclicity and the behavior of the operator $A$ in relation to its dual operator $A^*$. This research is an expansion upon the findings and concepts initially presented in the literature. It is worth noting that the term "codiskoidal space" is an alternative to the more commonly used term "hyperbolic space", as it was employed in the original source. The equivalent terms will be used interchangeably throughout this document. The codiskoidal property can be defined in an invariant manner in relation to the action of isometries on the space. This research was inspired by the codiskyclicity of the shift operator on certain types of continuous functions. It forms an extension to the preliminary version that was presented at the 13th International Conference on Operator Theory, under the name of "Codiskyclicity of Operators on Infinite-Dimensional Spaces". Hyperparameter tuning in AI models, especially using methods like grid search, is common. Yet, these traditional techniques are impractical for most organizations due to the expense of training on private data sets. As a result, many rely on incremental learning, a process that uses previous training and combines it with new data to improve the model. Although effective, incremental learning typically requires the same dataset it was initially trained on to achieve optimal performance on a related task. This usual constraint limits its application where private data is involved. This study explores alternative hyperparameter settings that enable a model to perform well on a related task with minimal new data, without the need for access to the original private dataset. Experimental results on three IncLearn datasets show that our approach is indeed effective, with performance improving when applying it to tasks with similar amounts of new data. Moreover, our approach succeeds on datasets with different characteristics of data, further confirming its versatility. Overall, our approach provides a cost-effective, privately-trained model that can be easily adapted to meet changing demands. Quantum computers are still largely incompatible with most implementations of the HHL algorithm due to numerous qubit losses and gate errors. In response, we've developed the NISQ-HHL protocol, a modified HHL algorithm tailored for near-degenerate matrix inversion on low-quality, medium-capacity quantum devices. This NISQ-HHL algorithm leverages qubit reuse and incorporates various efficiency enhancements to efficiently execute the HHL variant on such devices, and our results show it can accurately solve a wide range of problems with up to $10^4$ qubit magnitude errors and $10^3$ gate approximations. Furthermore, the NISQ-HHL algorithm can be applied to solve inverse problems defined by linear systems with low-condition-number matrices, as well as generate truly random vectors and Gaussian-distributed vectors on quantum devices. Additionally, we've created a hybrid classical-quantum algorithm that uses the NISQ-HHL algorithm to solve a random linear system with a medium-sized matrix (approximately 20 qubits), and our experiments using the Google Quantum AI Lab's Sycamore processor show that the NISQ-HHL algorithm can reduce qubit requirements by up to 90% and execution time by up to 99% compared to a direct application of the HHL algorithm. The NISQ-HHL algorithm's performance also scales linearly with the number of qubits, and we believe it has the potential to efficiently solve a wide range of inverse problems on large-scale quantum devices. The NISQ-HHL algorithm is now publicly available as part of the Qiskit Terra SDK. The corresponding source code can be found at https://github.com/qiskit-education/nisq-hhl-education. We investigate the stochastic process of available parking spaces as it evolves over time in a growing one-dimensional grid, and we examine the distribution of the first k n available spaces, denoted as $\tau_k^n$, as it changes with time t. We establish that the time it takes for the first k n spaces to become available follows a negative binomial distribution, and we use this fact to calculate its expected value, variance, and standard deviation. We also determine the time it takes for all k n spaces to become available as minimum of k n independent exponential variables with rate n, which enables us to calculate its distribution, expectations, and standard deviations. We define two distances, the total variation distance and Kolmogorov distance, $\mathcal{TV}$ and $d_K$, between the distributions of $\tau_k^n$ and $\tau_k$, and we show that the distances satisfy $\mathcal{TV}^2(d_k^n,d_k) = \frac{k}{n+d kn}\frac{1}{n-1}$ and $d_K^2(d_k^n,d_k) = \frac{k^2}{(n+dk n)^2}\frac{1}{(n-1)^2}$. We also demonstrate that the total variation distance and Kolmogorov distance between the distributions of $\tau_k^n$ and $\tau_l^n$ are given by $\mathcal{TV}^2(d_k^n,d_l^n) = \frac{k-l}{(k-l n)\frac{1}{n-1}}$ and $d_K^2(d_k^n,d_l^n) = \frac{(k-l)^2}{((k-l)n)^2}\frac{1}{(n-1)^2}$. We prove that the distribution of the first k n places does not converge to a limit distribution as t tends to infinity, and we also show that the sequence of distributions is not ergodic. We establish that the sequence of distributions of the first k n places forms a renewal process with interarrival times given by a gamma distribution, and we use this fact to calculate the distribution of the first place that has become available for k n times as a pth renewal, which enables us to calculate its expectations, variance, and standard deviations. A promising concept for controlling the superconducting state through external electrical stimulation has been explored in nanowire sensors. Theoretical modeling suggests that the sensor's critical voltage can be adjusted by applying a voltage, and this adjustment can be permanent or reversible, depending on the intensity of the stimulation. Specifically, the model shows that the sensor's critical voltage can be modified within the 0 to 2V range by applying 0 to 1V stimulation, and this modification follows a non-linear relationship with a clear threshold at approximately 0.8V. The sensor's performance is assessed using figure-of-merit scores, with permanent modification resulting in a score of 10 and reversible modification scoring 5. The sensor's performance also deteriorates with increasing stimulation intensity, but improves when the applied voltage is the same as the critical voltage. The impact of the sensor's material properties and geometry on the performance and critical voltage adjustment is analyzed, with the interplay between two potential mechanisms - the formation of barriers at the sensor's contacts and the entry of defects during stimulation - also considered. The model's predictions are validated by simulation software and experimental data from nanowire sensors made from the nitinol alloy, with adjustable critical voltage proven in sensors with various geometries and materials. The model offers guidance for optimizing the sensor design to achieve a desired level of performance and critical voltage adjustment. The research demonstrates the practical feasibility of the concept, offering a versatile superconducting nanowire sensor that can be accurately modeled and designed. The model's limitations are discussed, along with potential future developments, including the creation of sensors with multiple adjustable states, the optimization of adjustable sensors, and the investigation of stimulation-induced defect diffusion in sensors with fixed critical voltage. The model can be applied to the development of nanowire sensors made from other materials, with the interplay between stimulation, material properties, and performance proven and quantifiable. The reliable prediction of sensor performance from material properties facilitates the transfer of knowledge from material science to nanowire sensors, representing a significant improvement over previous approaches. The research contributes to the development of superconducting nanowire sensors with adjustable critical voltage, providing a framework for optimizing sensors with fixed critical voltage and offering insights into the stimulation of sensors with fixed critical voltage, where the entry of defects during stimulation can be controlled to improve sensor performance. A video's novel view prediction enables the model to analyze both visual and temporal patterns and manipulate them to generate a new perspective. Despite the challenges it poses, recent advances in the topic have been made, largely focusing on representing videos through graphs and latent variables. In contrast, we've discovered that employing dual learning, a technique originally developed for translating language, significantly improves novel view prediction performance. Specifically, we've developed a novel dual learning framework for graph-based video representation, which involves creating two models: one that generates a video's novel view and another that predicts the original video from that view. Utilizing dual learning, our approach can produce views that are both more realistic and less prone to over-smoothing. In quantum mechanics, baryon mass spectra are understood using group theory, which assigns correct resonance patterns for different symmetries. However, determining how symmetries change over time has been a challenge. Using the Wigner-Eckart theorem and the complex rotation method, researchers have extracted the $1p$-shell mass spectrum for states like $N$, $O$, $S$, $A$, $K$, and $Sc$ from the Bethe-Salpeter equation, and have also analyzed the evolution of symmetries for the $D$-wave state in the $N$ nucleon scattering system. For the $N N$ system, they found that the mass shift follows the pattern $\frac{J(J-1)}{2}$ for $S$ and $D$-wave states, and has been compared with experimental and quark model data. Additionally, they have extracted the $3s$-shell mass spectrum for the $K$ state from the Bethe-Salpeter equation, which cannot be analyzed using the simple $\frac{J(J-1)}{2}$ pattern due to the presence of both $s$ and $d$-wave components. Furthermore, they have investigated the breaking of symmetries in the $3p$-shell mass spectrum for the $Sc$ state, which is crucial for understanding strange baryon mass spectra. Moreover, they have studied the time evolution of symmetries in the $N N$ system with a 3-body force, and have also analyzed the symmetries in the $Y N$ system, which cannot be described using the standard quark model due to the presence of both meson-baryon and baryon-triquark components. Finally, they have extracted the mass spectrum for the $K K$ system, which exhibits the desired $9j$-coupling symmetry, and has been compared with experimental and quark model data. We investigate how the $p$-norm used in a neural network affects its performance when optimizing a Lipschitz continuity constraint. Our investigation reveals that optimizing a $p$-norm-based Lipschitz constraint leads to a neural network that performs similarly to one optimized with the 2-norm-based Lipschitz constraint, despite requiring significantly more computational resources. To facilitate this comparison, we developed a general algorithm to enforce $p$-norm-based Lipschitz continuity and demonstrated the effectiveness of $p$-norms greater than 2, particularly $p=4$, in neural network training. When applying our approach to the task of binary classification using CIFAR-10, it showed promising results. Our method also compares favourably to existing approaches for enforcing Lipschitz continuity in neural networks. Our code is available online. When applying the 4-norm, our method achieves a binary classification accuracy of 93.13% on CIFAR-10, surpassing the current state of the art defined as the largest gain achieved through explicit regularization among existing methods, which is a 3.13% improvement over the standard neural network. To address this, our research introduces an enhanced NLO+PS approach that incorporates accurate NLO quark pair production and LEPTO-CONV-generated resonant leptoquark signals, utilizing CONNOR's clustering algorithm. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method for predicting phenomena related to vector leptoquarks with electroweak scale masses and reveal the significance of considering NLO corrections and precision jet production for the $SU(2)$ doublet vector leptoquark channel involving same-sign dilepton events. Furthermore, our analysis provides NLO+PS-optimized input parameters for vector leptoquark research involving same-sign dilepton and diphoton events. Additionally, our work highlights the NLO+PS methodology's broader applicability to other rare high-energy particle collisions. To facilitate the implementation of this method, our research is being made available through the LEPTO-CONV vector leptoquark generator framework. A Deep Neural Network (DNN) was developed to reduce PET image noise when only a low dose is used. In standard approaches, training and evaluation data must have the same image quality. Conversely, a method was proposed to use high-quality PET images and complementary MRI data to enhance low-dose PET images, without using middle-man reconstructed images. This DNN framework consists of two components: an encoder that extracts detailed and general image features, and a decoder that generates highly detailed images from the extracted features. During training, the DNN directly maps low-dose PET images and MRI data to high-quality PET images. This leads to better image enhancement, especially in the improvement of liver and kidney PET image quality based on contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) analysis. Moreover, the proposed method proves to be more effective than traditional reconstruction methods, especially in liver and kidney areas even after applying 20-dose of PET scans, without using additional training data. This DNN-based approach shows great potential in optimizing PET image acquisition parameters without sacrificing diagnostic accuracy. A code version of this research is available at https://github.com/NA-PET/DNN-PET-RADIX. A tutorial on implementing this method can be found in [1]. This study examines how contextualized word embeddings affect the performance of neural coreference resolution systems with a focus on centering theory. Despite the progress made in coreference resolution, many studies ignore the implications of centering theory for this task. To address this, we modified existing data preparations to utilize neural coreference resolution systems and evaluated them on the basis of centering theory's rationality principles. Our experiments showed that these systems often violate the principles of centering theory, but adding contextualized word embeddings improved the coreference relations they produced. However, certain inconsistencies persisted, and we found these systems frequently confused the coreference relations for certain grammatical functions such as subject and object. Moreover, our research revealed that the distribution of coreference relations generated by these systems differs significantly from real-world data, suggesting that the coreference relations learned by these systems are not entirely reliable. Ultimately, our study highlights the potential limitations of neural coreference resolution systems with regards to centering theory's rationality principles, despite their proven accuracy in other aspects. Our statistical models can be used by researchers and practitioners looking to further refine the coreference relations produced by these systems. Furthermore, our research on contextualized word embeddings provides a foundation for exploring other contextualized features that can improve the coreference relations learned by these systems. Our work was conducted using the BART neural coreference resolution system, and our code is available online for the benefit of the research community. This code allows users to reproduce our experiments, modify our models as needed, and apply our features to other coreference resolution systems. Re-estimating the geospatial distance between WiFi fingerprints is crucial for developing accurate mapping and localization systems.  Due to the time-consuming and costly nature of traditional measurement methods, incorporating functional distance predictions from machine learning models is promising.  In response to growing mobile data frequencies and more complex neural network architectures, larger model-based distance estimation approaches have been proposed, albeit these methods are challenging to scale for real-world applications, especially on small-scale fingerprint datasets.  To address this challenge, this paper introduces an innovative approach using lightweight neural networks that can efficiently predict distance between WiFi fingerprints with reduced computational requirements, allowing for seamless integration into real-time localization systems.  Experimental results, using a freely available large-scale indoor dataset, University Campus Map (UCM), showed that the proposed method exceeds the performance of conventional regression-based approaches, demonstrating accurate distance estimation capabilities with low overhead.  Specifically, this paper demonstrates how using the proposed method to recalculate UCM's distance matrix reduces localization system error by 35.6% and boosts system efficiency by 90.6% compared to traditional metric learning methods.  The scaleable nature of this method enables distance recalculation for large and dynamic datasets, facilitating the development of self-adaptive and efficient localization systems.  As a tangible example, this paper shows that recalculation of UCM's distance matrix leads to a localization system that requires half the amount of training data (15,000 vs. 30,000) to achieve the same accuracy level, further highlighting the method's versatility and performance.  In summary, this paper presents a cutting-edge, efficiency-oriented approach for estimating distance between WiFi fingerprints using lightweight neural networks, exhibiting superior performance and computationally lightweight characteristics that facilitate seamless integration into real-time localization systems, offering vast potential for application in various indoor mapping and localization scenarios.  To facilitate further development, the code and model for this approach have been made publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/HadiHosseini/DeepDistSync.  Moreover, to facilitate reproducibility, the used dataset University Campus Map (UCM) is publicly accessible at the following link: https://github.com/HadiHosseini/University-Campus-Map-UCM-Dataset.  Ultimately, this research and the associated datasets can serve as a foundation for developing self-adaptive and efficient localization systems in various indoor settings. Given a graph G = (V, E), the geodesic distance tractance problem involves finding the smallest integer k such that the metric dimension of a truncated version of G, obtained by removing edges with distance greater than k from the set of original vertices V, becomes 1. This involves formulating a combinatorial problem that is equivalent in complexity to an already known problem related to metric dimension. Our main result shows that a specific instance of this equivalence, related to a particular value of k = 2, has a distinct character compared to other instances of the same type, requiring a significantly larger number of computations even for much simpler cases. This is demonstrated through an algorithm that computes the answer for a specific value of k = 2, requiring an exponential number of computations, whereas an algorithm for the general case k >= 2 has a polynomial computational complexity. This general algorithm can be used as a prototype to understand different categories of instances. Our results also include a previous unpublished conclusion related to the geodesic distance domain size problem, a variant of the tractance problem, where the goal is to find the minimum integer k such that the number of domains of geodesic distance k in a graph G becomes 1. This involves determining if there are graphs that have an infinite number of domain distances, or if all graphs have a specific maximum domain distance value, particularly for graph types such as hypercubes and complete graphs. Our research presents three point spread function analysis methods that can be effective in detecting binary asteroids from wide field surveys like the Pan-STARRS1 database. These techniques involve comparing the brightness of an object to its surrounding field, which can help reveal the telltale signature of a binary asteroid as it transits its primary component. For objects detected within the survey's inner region, we used the average difference in brightness between the detected target and surrounding field as its characteristic feature. This approach was particularly useful for discovering binary asteroids among the survey's most sensitive detections. Alternatively, a variation of the Schuster variational method can be applied to a larger set of measurements, which we tested using a subset of the survey's outer region observations. This method involves comparing the variability of an object by examining the difference in brightness between its highest and lowest points of measurement. Additionally, we introduced a third approach that combines the advantages of both previous methods, combining the mean difference in brightness with the standard deviation of the variations of an object to identify binary asteroids. By employing these techniques on the Pan-STARRS1 survey data, we detected 0.83 binary asteroid candidates per million resolved pixels measured. This translates to approximately 130,000 binary asteroid candidates among the survey's detected population of approximately 156 million. However, only 0.01% of these candidates exhibit the characteristic signature of binary asteroids as they transit their primary components, suggesting that many small binaries may go undetected through survey-based research. Ultimately, our study reveals a significant potential in wide field surveys for identifying binary asteroids, particularly those with orbital periods less than a day, and suggests that the survey of the full sky for binary asteroids is feasible with current survey data, awaiting analysis. Our research also highlights the survey's inner region, the most sensitive area for detecting binary asteroids, as a more promising area of study, particularly for discovering asteroids with orbital periods greater than a day, for which the survey provides comprehensive data. Our proposed methods are not limited to the Pan-STARRS1 survey data, and we encourage the application of these techniques to other wide field surveys like the LSST survey, the survey of the southern sky with the VST survey, the Pan-STARRS2 survey, and the ATLAS survey. Our initial findings can be further developed through the analysis of existing survey data, and even more significant discoveries are expected from upcoming surveys of the sky. Our research provides a foundation for the survey-based identification of binary asteroids and offers various approaches that can be combined with other techniques currently in use

Our in-depth analysis of four "shallownot" proteins reveals a distinct folding paradigm compared to "deepnot" counterparts, and our research suggests this distinction arises from the interplay between knoting and hydrophobic interactions at the protein's early stages of folding. Unlike "deepnot" proteins, whose complex architectures delay until middle stages of folding, "shallownot" proteins quickly form basic beta-sheet structures, then gradually develop their intricate knotted forms through a slow process of ring-exchange reactions between sheet loops. By contrast, "deepnot" proteins' intricate structures emerge before they can adopt temporary, less stable sheet forms. Through the study of one "shallownot" protein, we found that specific hydrophobic interactions between distal parts of the protein drive its knoting process, offering a striking example of non-local interactions that guide protein folding. Our research emphasizes the significance of considering non-sequential ring-exchange reactions in protein folding models. Furthermore, our simulations of the one "shallownot" protein provide a detailed understanding of its knoting process, revealing that its specific architecture is the result of a delicate balance between repulsive electrostatic interactions and attractive hydrophobic forces. Our results have implications for understanding the folding of other knotted proteins and highlight the potential biases introduced by focusing solely on rapidly folding, "shallownot" proteins in protein folding research. Our comprehensive analysis of these proteins also reveals that their side chain configurations are more stable than those of non-knotted proteins, suggesting a possible link between protein knoting and the optimization of side chain interactions. Finally, our study reveals that protein knoting can result from the interplay of folding forces, even in the absence of any distal hydrophobic interactions, offering a broader perspective on this complex biochemical process. Our research was carried out using the GFRD-Ka contact protein folding simulator, a comprehensive tool that models all possible contact combinations between amino acids during protein folding. Our findings were validated through comparisons with experimental data from NMR structures of the one "shallownot" protein, ubiquitin cross-talking (UBC), and three "deepnot" proteins, as well as non-knotted reference proteins. Our research demonstrates the uniqueness of protein knoting processes and highlights the potential biases in protein folding research that prioritize fast-folding proteins. By focusing on knotted proteins, we have gained a more nuanced understanding of protein folding dynamics and the importance of considering non-sequential ring-exchange reactions and non-local interactions that guide protein folding. We establish an irrationality criterion for a symplectic form on a certain type of closed orientable manifold without a point to remove. This criterion can be applied to modify an irrational symplectic form on a specific class of manifolds while maintaining its topological characteristics. Specifically, this form can be altered to have a specific property - being asymptotically conformally flat - while the underlying manifold remains with an irrational symplectic form. This finding contradicts a recent main result from a paper by Desodis and Frascino, which previously claimed that a form satisfying the above-mentioned condition cannot exist on an infinite number of closed orientable manifolds without a point to remove. This discovery also opposes another result from the same paper, which stated that a form meeting a particular standard cannot be transformed into another form meeting another standard on a certain type of manifold without a point to remove, unlike what we have found. This new observation we have made holds true for the class of manifolds known as Vassiliev surfaces of order 3 or higher. This means that we can change the symplectic form on these manifolds to meet another condition while keeping its topological characteristics the same, but this cannot be done on the simplest type of these manifolds, known as the trefoil knot, which serves as our main example in this research. This trefoil knot case study allows us to illustrate all the key steps and reasons behind our new finding. Researchers who use graphene as a growth substrate for epitaxial materials often encounter a problem where different materials domains form during synthesis at a single temperature. To understand this complication, researchers who grow materials on graphene typically conduct post-synthesis analyses of the resulting epitaxial layers. In contrast, this study grows ferroelectric bismuth ferrite on graphene by chemical vapor deposition and observes the formation of different domains during growth at various temperatures. It was discovered that growth temperatures either low or high lead to the formation of uniform domain patterns, whereas intermediate temperatures result in random domains. Additionally, the thickness of the grown layers changes significantly with temperature, indicating that temperature affects not only the domain formation but also the layer thickness during growth on graphene. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that growth temperature affects both domain formation and layer thickness when growing bismuth ferrite on graphene by chemical vapor deposition. Given the importance of domain formation in determining the properties of materials, this study suggests that growth temperatures should be carefully controlled to achieve the desired properties in epitaxial materials grown on graphene. Furthermore, it was observed that cutting down the thickness of the grown layers leads to a switch in the preferred domain formation, either to random or uniform patterns, indicating that layer thickness serves as another important factor that influences domain formation during growth on graphene. Nonetheless, cutting down the layer thickness also results in a significant decrease in the area of uniform domains, making it necessary to balance layer thickness with domain formation in search of optimal conditions. Ultimately, this study lays the ground for exploring the relationship between domain formation, layer thickness, and other growth parameters on graphene. A novel approach called single-to-multi (S2M) sampling is proposed to generate multi-label data with superior quality and minimal labeling expenses. A single labeled instance can be used to generate a set of related labeled instances, all connected by the same set of labels. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of S2M sampling, a critical assessment of existing data generation techniques is conducted from the perspective of labeling costs. Portfolio management strategies for cloud computing resources are influenced by optimization techniques, and researchers are continually developing more effective methods. This study examines utility and multi-objective optimization approaches for cloud portfolios and resources, and it also introduces two novel optimization methods: a portfolio-based approach for managing resources and a hybrid approach that combines utility and multi-objective optimization. The results show that the novel methods reduce costs and increase utility more effectively than existing methods. In the context of recruitment, scheduling interviews and assembling panels can be a complex task. This problem shares similarities with other logistics challenges, including vehicle routing and timetabling, which have been addressed using algorithmic solutions. However, a lack of suitable algorithms for interview scheduling and panel creation has been observed, forcing recruiters to rely on manual methods for arranging interviews, which can be both time-consuming and inefficient. This paper introduces two novel algorithms to enhance the efficiency of this process. The first algorithm, designed for a static scenario, generates a optimal schedule by leveraging a two-step approach following an initial random placement phase. This algorithm has multiple advantages, including the ability to accommodate preferences for panel members and interviewers, as well as the ability to minimize delays between interviews. The second algorithm, suited for a dynamic scenario, incorporates elements of the first algorithm within a more comprehensive framework that also incorporates a panel creation module and an acceptance policy for appointments. Both algorithms have been put through computational trials using real-world data, and the results show a significant improvement over existing, non-automatic methods, with the dynamic algorithm demonstrating higher efficiency scores due to its ability to adapt to changing conditions, such as changes in availability of panel members and interviewers. In one example, the dynamic algorithm was able to create an optimal schedule for a hundred interviews with a panel of three members for each interview, generating a total of 300 task assignments, within one second. This improved schedule could be used with minimal modifications, indicating a significant benefit for organizations relying on algorithmic approaches to manage their interview scheduling and panel creation processes. Experimental data, together with the code and results, is available at https://github.com/HusseinAboourrod/Interview_Scheduling_Panel_Creation, and demonstrates the practical application of this research to real-world logistics challenges. The term "algorithmic approach" is interpreted broadly to include any non-manual method for arranging interviews, such as those based on integer programming, simulated annealing, and genetic algorithms. The initial research encountered difficulties with integer programming, leading to the adoption of a random placement phase within the two-step algorithm used in the current paper, which resulted in a significant improvement in its performance. This research investigates an extended backward stochastic differential equation (BSEDD) that accounts for a underlying diffusion, denoted as the reference BSEDD, and provides a solution to a payoff optimization problem. We establish the connection between the extended BSEDD and the original BSEDD, and show that the optimal payoff is linked to the solution of the original BSEDD with a modified final value. Furthermore, we derive an optimal control problem for forward stochastic differential equations (FSEDD) and demonstrate that the optimal payoff can be achieved through the solution of this FSEDD. The final result involves a connection between the original BSEDD and an FSEDD with a constant drift term. The study also explores relationships between the original and extended BSEDD, including convergence results. These connections enable us to establish the uniqueness of the solution to the original BSEDD, as well as the convergence of the solution to the extended BSEDD. The study also addresses the case where the underlying diffusion is multi-dimensional. This research is an extension of previous studies on the optimal payoff in the context of backward stochastic differential equations, and provides an alternative proof of the uniqueness of the solution to the original BSEDD. The approach used here also builds on previous diffusion approximation methods. The statistical application considered in this research is related to the optimal portfolio payoff in stochastic differential equity pricing models. This leads to a reference BSEDD with a constant drift term, and its connection to an FSEDD can be found in the work of Jiang and Dyrghe (2013). This research extends the one-dimensional underlying diffusion case studied in the work of Jiang and Dyrghe (2013) to a multi-dimensional underlying diffusion. This enables us to model stock prices in multiple asset classes using the approach used here. Our analysis focuses on approximate analytic expressions for the power spectral density (PSD) of signals from individual relativistic binary sources and pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). We evaluated three factors: precision, complexity, and applicability to PTA experiments. The approximate expressions showed a 10,000-fold decrease in computation time versus existing numerical methods and similar accuracy to other techniques used in PTA data analysis. For gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers, we found that the precision of approximate models varies significantly across different phases of the orbits, primarily due to the varying importance of post-merger oscillations. This research examines the ASEP system with two distinct particle types to investigate the system's dynamics. A mathematical equation, derived from the ASEP model, allows us to track the movement of a particular second-class particle. As time passes, the movement of this particle becomes increasingly random, eventually conforming to a normal distribution. A third class of particles is introduced to enhance system randomness, and we employ discrete probability distributions to study the relationship between these particles and the second-class particles. Our study reveals that the combination of these particles generates different time-based velocity distributions. Our research creates a viable effective non-rigid pendulum model to simulate the behavior of a specific quantum system, comprised of two coupled optical lattices implementing atom-molecule conversions, even under strong coupling. This non-rigid pendulum model is uniquely defined by considering the relative population between atoms and molecules as its oscillatory variable. By employing this model, we explore both its individual components and combined components for both one- and two-dimensional configurations. Our findings reveal the existence of mode-locking patterns of dynamical behavior within the non-rigid pendulum model, thereby indicating the existence of stable atom-molecule patterns in the corresponding optical lattice system. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the onset of instabilities in a quantum system can be accurately predicted by analyzing the rigid pendulum's dynamics, with modifications needed for the mode-locking regime. Additionally, we demonstrate that by adjusting the coupling between components, the model itself can undergo atom-molecule phase transitions in both one- and two-dimensional configurations. Our non-rigid pendulum model exhibits the ability to simulate atom-molecule phase transitions in optical lattices, offering a straightforward and dynamic framework for understanding the associated complex behaviors and related instabilities. Ultimately, this model provides a promising tool for predicting and analyzing the behavior of atom-molecule conversions in optical lattices. Our study also highlights the versatility of non-rigid pendulum dynamics in capturing the complex behaviors of a specific quantum system, thereby demonstrating the generality of this model. Our research reveals that the non-rigid pendulum dynamics of the atom-molecule system rely heavily on the intermolecular interaction between components, which can be adjusted to vary the rigidity of the pendulum dynamics itself. Consequently, our findings underscore the significance of considering the composite nature of relevant quantum systems in order to accurately predict their dynamics and phase transitions. Our effective non-rigid pendulum model also exhibits the ability to simulate two coupled Bose-Jensen-Hubbard (BJH) systems, which can be realized using current technological capabilities. By exploring both individual components and combined components of both one- and two-dimensional configurations, our study reveals the existence of stable atom-molecule patterns, which can arise through a phase transition controlled by the intermolecular interaction between components. Our research demonstrates that the onset of instabilities in the BJH system can be accurately predicted by analyzing the rigid pendulum's dynamics, with modifications needed for the mode-locking regime. A key challenge in DNA data storage systems involves managing storage partitions, as they require for encoded data to be divided into manageable blocks of DNA fragments. To efficiently retrieve data, a well-designed method for creating primer pairs is proposed, along with a algorithm for generating partitions, to ensure that all pairs efficiently target specific blocks of fragments, thereby reducing storage costs. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this design, experiments were conducted using real-world applications, showing a significant improvement over existing methods. Furthermore, to facilitate practical implementation, the proposed method's limitations and potential solutions are explored. Additionally, possible pathways for decoding multi-block sets are presented, along with an evaluation of these methods. To facilitate widespread use, the proposed method's source code has been made publicly available on a relevant repository, showcasing the feasibility of the design and encouraging further customization. To enhance the practicality of DNA data storage, possible customization options for primer pairs are investigated, including those that minimize fragment length variations and those that prioritize decoding specific multi-block sets. Lastly, the proposed method's limitations are discussed, along with strategies for addressing them, such as sorting blocks before decoding or employing additional encoding schemes. Lastly, possible future directions for improving the primer pairs design are explored, along with an invitation to collaborate on developing a standard for DNA data storage. Recently, a growing number of images have been captured using multi-frame HDR techniques, and these images are being shared on social media platforms.  These platforms typically use single-image retouching technology to enhance image quality, but this method alone is not sufficient to produce multi-frame HDR images.  Existing research has demonstrated that it is possible to create HDR images using a single image and a limited set of input parameters, but these methods require additional images and detailed metadata.  In contrast, our novel approach, SESS, is a first-of-its-kind algorithm that can enhance single-image HDR without relying on additional data.  We introduced a new metric, the Exposure Stretch Score (ESS), to automate evaluation and feedback.  ESS assesses the visual appeal of an image by considering factors like contrast, brightness, and the presence of overly dark or overly bright areas.  To achieve the desired level of excellence, we employed a multi-frame HDR image generation network in combination with a contrast-aware loss function and two secondary agents that leveraged contrast and ESS scores.  Furthermore, we developed a seamless automatic exposure setting selection method using a mixture of uniform distribution and exponential distribution as the probability density function (PDF) to ensure the algorithm's robustness across various platforms.  Our results show that our approach can create stunning HDR images from a wide range of input images, outperforming existing single-image HDR techniques like LDR to HDR, PTM, and Panaltd, as well as multi-frame HDR techniques like GFDNet and DeepHDR.  Our research and proposed approach provide a foundation for future advancements in single-image HDR technology. Causal deep learning methods aim to integrate causal knowledge with deep learning, potentially leading to a significant reduction in data requirements and improvements in model reliability. However, the diversity of these methods makes it challenging to identify gaps in research. This paper organizes diverse causal deep learning methods using a unified framework, revealing unexpected connections and significant research gaps, particularly in categories related to model selection and performance evaluation. This effort is a initial step towards fostering collaboration among researchers in the field. This is because, despite significant progress in natural language processing, there is still much to be explored in relation to the causal aspects of its theories, datasets, and algorithms. This paper is thus a first call for participation in the field of natural language processing that is informed by causal principles. This is achieved through an inclusive and representative research agenda that encompasses multiple subfields of natural language processing. This agenda is guided by three core pillars: incorporating causal information to enhance performance, improving understanding of the inherent structures of language through causal analysis, and using natural language to efficiently acquire causal knowledge with various sources. This paper also presents an original compilation of actionable research ideas, concrete problems to be solved, and novel approaches that can be tested through innovative experiments. This is demonstrated by applying various natural language processing techniques to tasks such as sentence interpretation, language modeling, text generation, paraphrasing, summarization, and microtext classification, and assessing their performance across multiple metrics including model selection, evaluation methods, and datasets. This paper also examines potential sources of causal knowledge including dictionaries, ontologies, lexical databases, documents, texts, and oral communications, evaluating their reliability, availability, and accessibility for use in natural language processing tasks. This is further explored through qualitative and quantitative analyses of language theories, evaluation of research gaps, and innovative applications. This paper also delves into the scalability of natural language processing tasks that incorporate causal principles, assessing the additional computational cost and memory requirements across various methods and datasets. This is demonstrated by conducting repeated experiments under different conditions, analyzing the underlying factors, and proposing potential solutions to improve the efficiency of these tasks. We develop a new model that incorporates Gaussian diffusion with correlations and heterogeneity, which we call the correlated Gaussian diffusion model. We then apply this model to the spread of H1N1 in China during 2005, a system that has been shown to be highly connected and varied. By comparing our model to traditional Gaussian diffusion models, we have found that it better explains the observed spread patterns, particularly in accounting for the slow start of the epidemic. Additionally, the proposed model performs well in predicting future epidemic data when compared to other models. We have also tested our model on simulated data sets and found that it accurately predicts both small-scale and large-scale diffusion patterns. Therefore, the correlated Gaussian diffusion model presents a useful tool for predicting the spread of the epidemic in complex networks. We studied cross-phase modulation (XPM) and self-phase modulation (SPM) in a loop resonator with two identical counterpropagating modes. XPM was found to be 4 times stronger than SPM when utilizing the same input powers in both directions. This distinction leads to distinct spectral broadening patterns, with XPM producing a symmetric shift on either side of the original frequency, in contrast to SPM which results in an asymmetric shift. Furthermore, we observed that XPM predominantly occurs during the initial stage of a pulse, whereas SPM becomes more prominent towards the end of the pulse. Additionally, we noticed that higher order spectral broadening is more evident in XPM. These findings are valuable for optimizing pulse propagation within loop resonators, particularly in the context of supercontinuum generation. Furthermore, the distinct characteristics of XPM and SPM offer promising applications in the generation of non-linear spectral patterns. 

Moreover, we observed that the interaction between XPM and SPM can result in altered dynamic behaviors, depending on the initial phase differences between the counterpropagating modes. We found that a 180-degree initial phase difference prevents non-linear spectral broadening, while a 0-degree initial phase difference enables it. Furthermore, we discovered that the strength of both XPM and SPM can be significantly enhanced through the use of a narrow beam in comparison to a larger one, by reducing the interaction between the counterpropagating modes and minimizing the effect of the resonator's lossy components. This improvement can, however, be affected by the presence of non-linear components that generate new frequencies, which in turn interact with the original modes and alter the effective phase difference between them. We utilized numerical solutions to pulse propagation equations to demonstrate these phenomena, and verified these results with experimental data from a specific loop resonator. This research provides a foundation for exploring non-linear interactions within loop resonators in the context of optical confocal architectures.

Reinforcement learning algorithms are constantly evolving, and the necessity to continually assess their performance using automated methods has risen in step. We propose a novel evaluation framework that analyzes recent REINFORCE-based learners using simple curriculum learning, which provides a controlled picture of their developmental capabilities. The proposed curriculum learning task rewards agents for mastering a basic skill before being allowed to tackle an associated more challenging task that requires transfer learning abilities. We demonstrate that the framework's results effectively discern between different reinforcement learning methods, accurately reflecting their capacity for learning from feedback and adapting to new situations. Furthermore, we show that the proposed curriculum learning model serves as a plausible proxy for evaluating real-world applications, as it mimics the characteristics of natural learning curves observed in actual scenarios. We test the framework using multiple learning scenarios, including both simple and complex real-world examples, and the resulting data is available for download at the ReinLearnRepository. We hope the proposed evaluation method and associated results will contribute to a deeper understanding of how current reinforcement learning algorithms learn and adapt in complex environments, and to facilitating the development of more effective learners. We also offer the underlying curriculum learning model as a versatile tool that can be tailored to meet the needs of various real-world learning scenarios. We highlight the potential risks and considerations associated with automated performance evaluation, and stress the value of concurrently conducting human evaluations for cross-validation and to ensure the underlying learning curves remain trustworthy. We propose the term ``curriculum sensitivity'' to describe the framework's ability to accurately determine learning curves from automated evaluations, and we identify several key factors that influence curriculum sensitivity, including the design of learning tasks, the associated underlying data, and the availability of human evaluation options. We also outline a possible future direction for developing more reliable and automated methods of evaluating the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms using controlled curriculum learning tasks. Our proposed approach, called the Decoupled Contextual Reachability (DCR) graph, provides a framework for exploring the context of process changes by considering reachability analysis in process models. A DCR graph is a combination of a set of process models and the context in which they make sense, allowing for efficient identification of models that differ from a given set of patterns. Our approach ensures that only relevant models are considered, enabling significant computational cost savings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DCR graphs through experimental results showing they can handle large datasets of process models relative to other Decoupled Contextual Reachability (DCR) based approaches, including a significant reduction in computational time of up to 900x. Moreover, our technique has been applied to real-world processes at a leading technology firm, revealing that their actual process behavior diverged from their desired process model, particularly in contexts related to data integration and customer relationship management. Our results show that our method successfully identified the aspects of their process that require improvement. Our technique has been implemented as a part of the ProM framework, a renowned process analysis tool, and is available for public use through its website. We show that this moduli space receives a natural map from the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{1,1}(d)$, which is the space of one-pointed genus $g$ curves with a linear functional, by utilizing the technique of sectioning vector bundles. Both galaxies with higher masses than approximately one billion solar masses and low central black hole masses exhibit the same color, yet for galaxies with more massive black holes, the color becomes more red. This observation is consistent with previous findings in the field, but it became particularly evident when focusing on the most massive galaxies within each group. We propose that this pattern is attributed to the effects of quenching, as it is observed in field galaxies, where colors become more red above a certain mass threshold, often marked by the transition from giant ellipticals to ultra-massive ellipticals. This is further supported by data from SDSS and 4D-NGS, showing similar trends in NUV-r colors. Additionally, we observed a stronger quenching effect on the colors of galaxies within the most massive groups, likely due to their older ages and lower gas content. Therefore, we conclude that the effects of quenching scaling, coupled with age and chemical evolution, predominantly affect the NUV-r colors of the most massive galaxies within each group. We also note that the relationship between color and black hole mass is not unique to quenching, as it could be influenced by other factors such as age, metallicity, and environmental density. Nonetheless, we propose that the unique characteristics of ultra-massive ellipticals, shaped by their quenching history, differentiate them from other galaxy populations. This is particularly evident when comparing the CIG sample to the 4D-NGS, which includes a broader range of galaxy masses, allowing for a more in-depth analysis of this quenching scaling effect. This research has implications for ongoing and future missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, which, with its extended wavelength coverage, will be better suited to uncover the complexities of quenching in galaxy populations. This is especially true for NUV-r color, which, in the near-infrared, will be less susceptible to age and chemical evolution, allowing for a more direct understanding of the quenching process. This discovery also highlights the value of multi-wavelength observations, as a sole NUV-r color analysis might lead to incorrect conclusions, due to the influence of age, metallicity, and age-metallicity decomposition. Therefore, future studies should consider comprehensive analyses, incorporating additional parameters, and comparing different quenching populations with precise age and chemical abundance determinations.

Neural machine translation has seen significant advancements in recent years, thanks in part to the widespread use of LSTMs and NNs in model architectures. While substantial improvements have been observed within similar language groups, the disparity in performance is particularly notable when translating between languages of different families, such as Asian languages and European languages. Various techniques have been developed to tackle this challenge, including multi-way machine translation and cross-domain neural network models. One specific approach, using a common target language to bridge the gap between two different source languages, has been found to be particularly effective. In this research, a straightforward extension to this approach is presented, using two different source languages to learn a target language bridge that can be used for both translation tasks. When tested on a particular dataset, this model showed the best results compared to other methods, processing 36.57 bits per token at 20.00 tokens per second. Additionally, a detailed analysis of model performance was conducted, revealing that models perform best on languages with minimal grammatical differences, and that models can be used to classify the sentiment of text from a different language, without the need for retraining. Furthermore, the examination of model consistency was performed, using the same dataset to train multiple models, and comparing the results with no significant difference found. In terms of applications, this model has been used in multiple scenarios, including the translation of user input, the generation of abstracts, and the classification of text from a different language, showing particular promise in these areas. In terms of limitations, the model can be challenging to implement, requiring a substantial amount of data, as well as significant computational resources. Nevertheless, the presentation of this model is aimed at contributing to the broader discussion of model generalizability, with the model's source code being made available publicly for use and modification by others. Furthermore, various techniques are proposed to enhance the model, including the incorporation of neural language models, the usage of intermediate languages, and the integration of rule-based knowledge, with the potential to enhance the model's performance further. In conclusion, the presentation of this model is aimed at sparking debate on the generalizability of models, with the potential to contribute to the advancement of models in the field of neural machine translation. In terms of future work, possible areas of improvement are identified, with the potential to enhance the model through the inclusion of neural language models, the usage of intermediate languages, and the integration of rule-based knowledge, among other possibilities. The model's source code is being made available publicly for use and modification by others

A critical challenge in addressing the COVID-19 pandemic lies in allocating limited resources effectively, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs).  To tackle this issue, it's essential to analyze data related to patients' features, including their ICU admission details.  We propose a novel resource allocation strategy that aims to maximize the number of treatments for COVID-19 patients by sorting them based on their risk of dying from the disease.  To evaluate this approach, we conducted an empirical study using data from New York, spanning from March to May 2020.  The results showed that our proposed method could treat up to 15.6% more patients in an ICU with the same capacity, and this difference was significant according to a two-sample t-test.  Furthermore, our strategy yielded better performance than random allocation in almost all scenarios tested.  A key finding from the data analysis revealed that deaths outside ICUs are 1.34 times more frequent than deaths within ICUs in New York.  To further optimize our model, we suggested sorting patients based on their location of admission, with those outside receiving lower priority.  The implications of our study extend beyond the COVID-19 context to other life-or-death emergencies such as severe burns or massive trauma, where a strategic approach to allocating ICU slots could be beneficial.  To facilitate this kind of analysis in the future, we propose integrating feature analysis into the study of resource allocation problems.  To enhance the reproducibility of our study, we are providing the code and methodology used to conduct the research, along with the relevant data, in a public repository available on GitHub.  This endeavor is an extension of our previous research presented at the 24th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, held in August 2021 in Bangkok, Thailand.  That initial study led to follow-up research mentioned in this paper.  We are making this code and data freely available in the hope that it will be useful for related research and to contribute to the ongoing global fight against the COVID-19 pandemic.  We are also providing the presentation slides and a video recording of the related research presented at the International Conference on Artificial Intelligence for further reference.  Moreover, we are making the related data from New York freely available in the hope that it will be beneficial for future research, according to the relevant guidelines and regulations.  This data is part of a larger dataset made available by the New York State Governor's Office, which can be accessed through the official website of the New York State COVID-19 Data Portal. Galaxies forming for the first time are subject to gravitational influence by nearby
masses, leading to the formation of accretion streams that shape the galaxies' evolution.
A computational study employs a highly advanced, memory-efficient hybrid N-body
technology to model these developments for a variety of environments. Unlike previous
research, accretion streams in this study remain intact for millions of years, allowing
observation of specific patterns of galaxy growth. The study identifies distinct patterns
of galaxies with unique characteristics, such as massive galaxies with distinct, swirling
disk components, to ones with slowed development having wispy, stellar halos. Another
observable effect of accretion streams is the creation of massive black holes at the
points where streams intersect the galaxies' cores. This discovery could explain the
observed close relationship between black holes and galaxies overall, despite absence of
such a correlation among younger galaxies. Another notable finding shows that galaxies
formed in the early universe are missing a specific type of metal enrichment, as if
stream-fed growth has favored elements like iron and magnesium over oxygen and
neon-rich materials. This phenomenon could also be accounted for by other processes,
but one that occurs in the present day's galaxy formation simulations is the presence of
central massive black holes. This achievement is valued as important future research,
paving the way for more intricate models that incorporate the formation of black holes
and stars within the same computational framework. The software used in this research
is available for public use, along with the underlying data, on the NYU Research Portal. 
The findings of this study are relevant to higher-resolution models of galaxy formation.

Fake news has been a rising concern on social media platforms, and the pandemic exacerbated this issue. Our proposed framework, MetaFEND, is an example of a robust framework that is tailored to detect high-quality fake news. The key innovation of MetaFEND lies in its capacity to generate complementary information that can be used in conjunction with natural text features to detect fake news. This is achieved by training a deep neural network to identify subtle, high-level patterns inherent to authentic texts, which it then uses to generate a compact, categorical representation of genuine writing styles. When combined with traditional text-based methods, this complementary information enhances the detection of fake news, surpassing the performance of existing approaches according to the FEVER fact-checking dataset. Our research also reveals that the incorporation of this complementary information can be optimized using a novel application of label noise, and this is demonstrated on the Enron spam email dataset, showing improved results compared to traditional approaches. Our proposed MetaFEND framework and the associated methods are now available as part of the deep learning repository at https://github.com/mostafalab/metafend. Our research provides a foundation for exploring various aspects of the detection of high-quality fake news, and it is anticipated that this topic will continue to garner significant interest from the machine learning community. Our findings are valid for the specific datasets FEVER and Enron, while the underlying concepts of the MetaFEND framework offer broader applicability to other written language phenomena. Our approach is distinctive from existing research on fake news detection, which focuses primarily on utilizing natural text features that underpin machine learning models. By contrast, our proposed framework exploits the inherent capabilities of deep neural networks to capture the nuanced, high-level patterns inherent to written language, and it leverages this complementary information to enhance the detection of fake news. Our research demonstrates that the incorporation of this complementary information can be optimized using a novel application of label noise, and this is demonstrated on the Enron spam email dataset, showing improved results compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, the paper provides an alternative interpretation of the modified equation through the study of a specific third-order parabolic system. The study of this system reveals that despite having odd initial data, solutions can become infinite in specific periods that are not half the distance between critical points. A quaternary Golay complementary array pair can be conceptualized as a method to create both Golay complementary arrays and Steinier chains from given parameters, providing a means to generate specific quaternary sequences while ensuring compliance with Golay's complementary property. For an array pair to be considered feasible, certain conditions involving the modulo operator and additive inverse must be met by the underlying parameters. This paper delves into the detail of how to construct array pairs satisfying the Golay property and offers a computational method to determine feasible parameter sets. Furthermore, we show that for a given set of parameters, it is possible to determine the feasibility of corresponding parameter sets. This feasibility is demonstrated through explicit examples and chain constructions, and we also provide a theoretical analysis of the relationship between array pairs and chains. Additionally, this paper explores additional relationships between four-letter sequences, binary chains, and Golay's complementary property, revealing that all binary chains can be generated from quaternary chains and offering a complementary perspective on the property of Golay compatibility. Researchers are seeking a reliable method to exchange interaction control in silicon based quantum devices by utilizing phosphorus impurities. To understand the effects of dopants at various locations, we investigated the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction in a silicon crystal lattice with multiple phosphorus atoms. Our study used a tight-binding method to analyze the effects of exchange interaction and direct coupling between spin and orbital motion. We found that the exchange interaction can be either facilitated or hindered by the placement of dopants, depending on the distance between them. Furthermore, we identified three distinct regimes of exchange interaction: atomic, strong coupling, and weak coupling. Our research provides a dopant placement strategy that can minimize exchange interaction and directly couple spin and orbital motion, potentially enhancing the capabilities of silicon based quantum devices. Our method involves placing dopants at sites with odd atomic number layers in silicon. Our study suggests that such placement can meet the requirements for both facilitated exchange interaction and direct coupling between spin and orbital motion. Consequently, we propose a device design that incorporates a Weyl semimetallic state in silicon by utilizing multiple phosphorus atoms. Our predictions are supported by computational simulations using a plane-wave based method within the framework of the pseudopotential approach. We demonstrated the feasibility of our proposed device design by analyzing its exchange interaction and direct coupling components. Our study paves the way for exploring the interplay between exchange interaction, direct coupling, and orbital motion in silicon based quantum devices incorporating multiple phosphorus atoms. Our proposed device design also exhibits a 10 times greater exchange time than silicon with single phosphorus atoms, and our predictions are consistent with experimental results involving ensemble spin-orbit coupling. Our research opens up possibilities for controlling exchange interaction, direct coupling, and orbital motion in silicon based quantum devices by adjusting dopant placement. We proposed such a device to a theoretical researcher from the University of New South Wales, Australia. Our study also compared the exchange interaction components with and without considering the direct coupling between spin and orbital motion in silicon based quantum devices incorporating multiple phosphorus atoms. We found that the exchange interaction time remains essentially unchanged, whereas the direct coupling component can change by a factor of 100, indicating that the direct coupling component has a more pronounced effect on the capabilities of such devices. Our research was featured in the cover page of the journal Physical Review Applied. We also presented our study at the Australian Institute of Nuclear Scientists and Engineers annual conference in Adelaide, Australia. Our research was supported by the Australian Research Council (ARC) through the ARC Centre of Excellence for Quantum Computation and Communication Technology

We introduce a novel method that utilizes a dynamic Bayesian network to model the system, and employs a meta-learning algorithm to train a classifier that identifies the most likely parent configuration for each time point, which is then used to guide future inferences through a weighted graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to simulated data, as well as real-world examples involving a nonlinear stochastic process and electric power grid data. This paper introduces a concept of weak flatness for graded polynomial rings in relation to certain algebras, then applies this to explore the stable homotopy theory of specific algebras, including those associated with partitions. Specifically, it demonstrates that graded polynomial rings are weakly flat with respect to an algebra (H$\Lambda$,T) if and only if the module extension problem (p)(Fp[\xi], T, H\Lambda) is trivial for all prime numbers p. It also examines connections to classical results on the homotopy types of (S^1)\ZZ and (S^1+\{0\})\ZZ. Furthermore, it develops methods to determine the weak flatness of graded polynomial rings for specific algebras (H$\Lambda$,T), including those linked to partitions, and uses these methods to investigate the ring structure and associated cohomology for these partitions. Ultimately, it utilizes these findings to interpret the ring structure and cohomology of the algebras (H$\Lambda$,T) as being composed of distinct, progressively complex parts, each corresponding to a particular manner of arranging natural numbers. This prequel to a larger project, builds upon earlier work displayed in the paper "On the Homotopy Types of the Boraowski-Burns Spaces" by the same author. It is worth noting that this research stems from the advice of W.G. Dwyer, J.M. Klein, and L. K. Conrad, along with conversations with H. Miller, C. Wilkins, and J. Neenhan. It is also noted that the term "partition" in this context refers to a sequence of natural numbers that add up to a given value, arranged in a specific order, rather than a classification of integers into sums of powers, as seen in another mathematical context. It is observed that the stable homotopy theory of these partitions can be interpreted through the use of graded polynomial rings and Alper's theory of weakly flat algebras, along with connections to the ring structure and cohomology of these partitions, providing a comprehensive framework that will be further developed in the companion paper "On the Homotopy Types of the Boraowski-Burns Spaces". However, a slowdown in program performance remained unchanged at 3 orders of magnitude behind native compilation, likely due to the overhead of functional operations. Deep neural networks have excelled in various classification tasks and have done so with a high level of accuracy. Nonetheless, the extracted features for classification purposes are not necessarily meaningful or representative of the underlying data patterns, as they are primarily tailored to the specific classification problem at hand. This issue is particularly pronounced in unsupervised learning, where the primary objective is to extract a meaningful representation of the input data without classification guidance. To address the limitations of current deep learning methods, we present a novel, multi-resolution deep embedding framework that efficiently handles both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. Unlike existing techniques that concentrate on a single representation, our proposed model leverages multiple representation layers to capture varying aspects of the input data, thereby enhancing the robustness and generalization of the extracted features. To achieve efficient feature extraction, we introduce a layer-by-layer sparsity constraints that reduce the number of parameters and operational complexity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, achieving performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple performance metrics. Nonetheless, it is noteworthy that the model's performance variability may depend on specific task parameters. Our proposed model is applicable to a wide range of applications, including image classification, where it can be used to extract local features, and on graph classification datasets such as the one presented in this study. These groups, termed $S_{\infty}$ and $A_{\infty}$, comprise permutations that preserve a specific graph structure and form compact, globally accessible subsets of the infinite permutation group. A noteworthy example illustrating the concept of a graph having an $S_{\infty}$-automorphism group is provided, involving a specific construction of infinite trees under particular branchifying processes. The frequency-domain sub-network uses a complex-valued extension of the Convolution Recurrent Network (CRN) to facilitate real-time speech enhancement with an efficiently computed spectrogram, thus minimizing computational costs. The time-domain sub-network, with its simpler convolutional structure, reduces circular padding issues common in recurrent networks. Evaluations conducted on the DPCRN outperformed existing time and frequency domain speech enhancement techniques in various conditions and datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency. Furthermore, a time-domain DPCRN was successfully applied to real-time speech enhancement, showcasing the framework's versatility. A basic two-fluid model is proposed to explain the heat transfer characteristics in convective flows by assigning a stable fluid to the convecting cells and an unstable fluid to the stable layers. The model assumes a perfect interface between the fluids and derives a simplified equation that matches the convective flow's behavior. By applying the model to a scenario with a horizontal bottom plate and an inclined top plate, researchers found that it predicts the significant increase in heat transfer for an angle up to 45 degrees from the model's own critical angle. Furthermore, the model successfully explains the increased heat transfer for small angles as being directly proportional to the square root of the angle. The model also shows that the heat transfer it predicts conforms to a power law when the angle is less than the critical angle, with an index that matches the findings of previous experiments conducted by Grossman, in which the stable layers were made of water and the bottom plate was heated. The model's limitations are such that it fails to accurately predict heat transfer for angles greater than 45 degrees from the critical angle, where the shape of the convecting cells changes to pear-shaped, and it also does not account for the effects of the interface's friction. The model assumes that the temperature difference between the top and bottom plates is large enough such that the temperature of the interface does not significantly affect the convecting cells' behavior. The model's predictions for heat transfer also vary with the ratio of the velocities of the two fluids, with values ranging from 1 to 10. The model predicts that the heat transfer it predicts will approach the value obtained from the convecting cells' equation with a power index of 1.43, which is close to the value of 1.48 obtained from the convecting cells' equation with the fluid's velocity as a variable, but with a power index of 2, when the ratio of the velocities of the two fluids is 10.
